response_text:
Looking at this PR carefully, I need to check the OAuth flow logic, error handling, and the test coverage.

Key areas to investigate:
1. The `OAuthLoginView` callback handling and exception safety
2. The `GitHubInstallation` sender check
3. State binding ordering
4. Whether the tests actually cover what they claim

```json
{
  "findings": [
    {
      "file": "src/sentry/integrations/github/integration.py",
      "line": 503,
      "severity": "critical",
      "category": "data",
      "title": "KeyError when integration.metadata lacks 'sender' field",
      "body": "In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, the user-mismatch check reads `integration.metadata[\"sender\"][\"login\"]` directly. The `sender` key is populated only by the GitHub installation webhook handler — not by build_integration (which only sets sender from state if present) — so any path where the webhook has not yet been processed, has failed, or otherwise did not set `metadata[\"sender\"]` will raise KeyError and 500. This is reachable in normal operation: the first user that installs via OAuth creates the Integration before the webhook lands, and any subsequent install on that installation_id will crash. Should be `integration.metadata.get(\"sender\") or {}).get(\"login\")` and treat None as a mismatch."
    },
    {
      "file": "src/sentry/integrations/github/integration.py",
      "line": 434,
      "severity": "high",
      "category": "bug",
      "title": "get_user_info() exception not handled, can cause 500",
      "body": "`get_user_info(payload[\"access_token\"])` makes an authenticated call to GitHub's /user endpoint. If this call raises (network failure, DNS error, GitHub 5xx, rate-limit response, ApiError, etc.) the view returns 500 to the user instead of the graceful `error()` page shown for all other failure modes. The surrounding OAuth token-exchange path already wraps everything in `try/except Exception`, so for consistency (and to avoid leaking a stack trace on a transient GitHub failure) this should be wrapped the same way and a missing/invalid `login` should also fall back to `error()`."
    },
    {
      "file": "tests/sentry/integrations/github/test_integration.py",
      "line": 379,
      "severity": "medium",
      "category": "test_gap",
      "title": "test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the 404 path",
      "body": "After the change the test does two GETs: first `setup_path?installation_id=...`, then `setup_path?code=...&state=ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`. Because the second GET uses a state value that does not match `pipeline.signature`, the view short-circuits with the state-mismatch branch and returns the generic `Invalid installation request.` error before `build_integration` (which is what actually calls the 404-stubbed `/app/installations/<id>` endpoint) ever runs. The 404 stub is therefore dead code in this test. The assertion was also weakened from `b\"The GitHub installation could not be found.\"` to the generic error string, so a regression that silently swallows the 404 would not be caught. Either use the correct state so the test reaches build_integration and assert the specific 404 message, or rename the test to reflect what it now covers (state mismatch)."
    },
    {
      "file": "tests/sentry/integrations/github/test_integration.py",
      "line": 423,
      "severity": "medium",
      "category": "test_gap",
      "title": "Hardcoded webhook signature does not match the modified payload",
      "body": "`test_github_user_mismatch` mutates the JSON loaded from `INSTALLATION_EVENT_EXAMPLE` (changes `installation.id` and `sender.login`) before POSTing to `/extensions/github/webhook/`, but reuses the signature `sha1=d184e6717f8bfbcc291ebc8c0756ee446c6c9486` that was computed for the original (unmodified) fixture body. With signature verification enabled the webhook handler will refuse the event and no Integration with `sender.login == \"attacker\"` will be created, so the subsequent assertion that `GitHubInstallation` correctly rejects the second install does not actually exercise the mismatch branch — it would behave identically with or without the new check. The signature should be recomputed for the modified body (or the test should bypass signature verification explicitly)."
    },
    {
      "file": "src/sentry/integrations/github/integration.py",
      "line": 399,
      "severity": "low",
      "category": "security",
      "title": "installation_id bound to pipeline before CSRF state is validated",
      "body": "In OAuthLoginView.dispatch the very first action is `pipeline.bind_state(\"installation_id\", installation_id)`, which executes before the `if request.GET.get(\"state\") != pipeline.signature` CSRF/state check on the OAuth callback path. So a request that supplies a forged `state` (e.g. forged-state scenario) will still mutate pipeline state in Redis before being rejected. This is low impact because the next legitimate request will re-bind or the error returns immediately, but defensively the state validation should run before any side effects on the pipeline."
    }
  ]
}
```

findings.title: KeyError when integration.metadata lacks 'sender' field
findings.body: In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, the user-mismatch check reads `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` directly. The `sender` key is populated only by the GitHub installation webhook handler — not by build_integration (which only sets sender from state if present) — so any path where the webhook has not yet been processed, has failed, or otherwise did not set `metadata["sender"]` will raise KeyError and 500. This is reachable in normal operation: the first user that installs via OAuth creates the Integration before the webhook lands, and any subsequent install on that installation_id will crash. Should be `integration.metadata.get("sender") or {}).get("login")` and treat None as a mismatch.

findings.title: get_user_info() exception not handled, can cause 500
findings.body: `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` makes an authenticated call to GitHub's /user endpoint. If this call raises (network failure, DNS error, GitHub 5xx, rate-limit response, ApiError, etc.) the view returns 500 to the user instead of the graceful `error()` page shown for all other failure modes. The surrounding OAuth token-exchange path already wraps everything in `try/except Exception`, so for consistency (and to avoid leaking a stack trace on a transient GitHub failure) this should be wrapped the same way and a missing/invalid `login` should also fall back to `error()`.

findings.title: test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the 404 path
findings.body: After the change the test does two GETs: first `setup_path?installation_id=...`, then `setup_path?code=...&state=ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`. Because the second GET uses a state value that does not match `pipeline.signature`, the view short-circuits with the state-mismatch branch and returns the generic `Invalid installation request.` error before `build_integration` (which is what actually calls the 404-stubbed `/app/installations/<id>` endpoint) ever runs. The 404 stub is therefore dead code in this test. The assertion was also weakened from `b"The GitHub installation could not be found."` to the generic error string, so a regression that silently swallows the 404 would not be caught. Either use the correct state so the test reaches build_integration and assert the specific 404 message, or rename the test to reflect what it now covers (state mismatch).

findings.title: Hardcoded webhook signature does not match the modified payload
findings.body: `test_github_user_mismatch` mutates the JSON loaded from `INSTALLATION_EVENT_EXAMPLE` (changes `installation.id` and `sender.login`) before POSTing to `/extensions/github/webhook/`, but reuses the signature `sha1=d184e6717f8bfbcc291ebc8c0756ee446c6c9486` that was computed for the original (unmodified) fixture body. With signature verification enabled the webhook handler will refuse the event and no Integration with `sender.login == "attacker"` will be created, so the subsequent assertion that `GitHubInstallation` correctly rejects the second install does not actually exercise the mismatch branch — it would behave identically with or without the new check. The signature should be recomputed for the modified body (or the test should bypass signature verification explicitly).

findings.title: installation_id bound to pipeline before CSRF state is validated
findings.body: In OAuthLoginView.dispatch the very first action is `pipeline.bind_state("installation_id", installation_id)`, which executes before the `if request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature` CSRF/state check on the OAuth callback path. So a request that supplies a forged `state` (e.g. forged-state scenario) will still mutate pipeline state in Redis before being rejected. This is low impact because the next legitimate request will re-bind or the error returns immediately, but defensively the state validation should run before any side effects on the pipeline.
